routes.description: Establish a personal transcendent creator through the universe's beginning, connect objective morality to a good divine foundation, and use the resurrection case to identify the creator with Christian theism, while showing that observed suffering and the evil-God analogy do not defeat that cumulative case.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its origin, moral, and resurrection components jointly support the Christian God and if the evidential inference from suffering is undercut by morally sufficient reasons or limits on human probability judgments without leaving the evil-God hypothesis evidentially symmetrical.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative arguments must support the existence of the Christian God strongly enough to withstand both the evidential problem of suffering and the evil-God symmetry challenge.

centralBridges.description: The universe's beginning must warrant a transcendent, immaterial, timeless, powerful, personal cause rather than mere unexplained origin.
Objective moral values and duties must require a divine foundation capable of supplying the creator's good moral character.
The historical resurrection case must discriminate in favor of divine action and connect generic creator reasoning to specifically Christian theism.
Apparently gratuitous suffering and the mirrored evil-God hypothesis must not warrant rejection of a good God once the full cumulative case and possible divine purposes are considered.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Human cognitive and historical limitations must materially constrain judgments that particular suffering lacks a morally sufficient providential purpose.
Divine goodness must rest on grounds other than a simple inductive inventory of worldly goods if the observational mirror is to misdescribe the theistic inference.

routes.description: Use the scale of apparently gratuitous suffering to disconfirm an omnipotent good God, show that standard defenses and appeals to inscrutable purposes transfer to an evil creator, and contest whether the cosmological, moral, and resurrection arguments supply the asymmetry or cumulative support required for Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if suffering remains substantial evidence against the good-God hypothesis, Craig's defenses fail to distinguish it from the parallel evil-God hypothesis, and the affirmative arguments do not independently establish the creator's goodness or specifically Christian identity strongly enough to overcome that challenge.

motionBridge.description: Observed suffering and evil-God symmetry must prevent Craig's cumulative arguments from establishing the good Christian God specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: The quantity, intensity, and history of sentient suffering must provide evidential grounds for excluding an omnipotent and perfectly good deity.
Free will, stable laws, soul-making, compensation, and unknown-purpose defenses must be shown to transfer materially from a good God to an evil creator.
The moral argument must fail to establish a divine foundation for objective morality capable of breaking the good-God and evil-God symmetry.
The cosmological and resurrection arguments must fail to identify a good Christian God or to outweigh the observational evidence invoked against that hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Rational exclusion of a specified deity must remain possible even without a complete alternative explanation of cosmic origins or suffering.
The evidential challenge must be formulable through excessive suffering without presupposing objective evil or the moral realism disputed by the moral argument.

sections.title: Cosmological Cause and the Creator's Moral Character
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the universe's beginning establishes a personal transcendent creator and whether that conclusion contributes anything toward choosing between a good creator, an evil creator, and a morally unspecified cause.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Its Proposed Divine Foundation
sections.rationale: The moral argument is the principal bridge from a morally neutral creator to divine goodness, while its premises, atheist-compatible alternatives, and relationship to suffering determine whether it can break the central symmetry.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Christian Identification
sections.rationale: The resurrection argument supplies the specifically Christian component of the cumulative case, making the reliability and discriminatory force of extraordinary historical testimony necessary issues rather than merely generic evidence for a creator.

sections.title: Suffering, Feasible Worlds, and Morally Sufficient Reasons
sections.rationale: The scale of sentient suffering is the principal observational evidence against a perfectly good God, and the dispute over feasible alternatives, providential purposes, and human epistemic limits directly governs that inference.

sections.title: Evil-God Symmetry and Observational Inference
sections.rationale: The defining comparative challenge asks whether defenses of a good God can be mirrored for an evil creator and whether observation may exclude a morally specified deity without serving as a positive argument for its opposite.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because the universe began to exist, it has an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, and personal transcendent cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig at the podium, and the uninterrupted opening address remains his until the next speaker transition.

response.rationale: Constructive opening move; it supplies the principal origin inference from the universe's beginning to a transcendent personal cause and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops an indispensable central bridge through an explicit deductive structure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion and its attributes are recoverable, though the transition from timeless immaterial cause to personal agency is compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The syllogistic conclusion follows if its premises hold, but the personal-cause extension is asserted more strongly than the excerpt's warrant establishes.

charity.alternative: A transcendent cause could be impersonal or otherwise unlike a personal creator.
charity.decisiveQualification: The deductive core establishes a cause only if both premises hold; personality requires a further bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stated syllogism is valid, but the move leaves a material bridge from transcendent cause to personal agency insufficiently developed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies philosophical and scientific support for a beginning, yet the selected evidence compresses premise defense and the personal-cause warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge concerning a transcendent personal cause and sits at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the need to derive attributes from the cause's nature but does not fully handle the strongest impersonal-cause alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly states the two premises, the necessary conclusion of a transcendent cause, and attributes that cause as uncaused, changeless, timeless, and immaterial.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties exist and require God as their transcendent foundation, thereby supporting God's existence and goodness.
moves.attributionBasis: This numbered argument occurs within Craig's uninterrupted opening address after his cosmological case and before his historical case.

response.rationale: Constructive opening move; it presents the moral argument as the bridge from a generic creator to divine goodness and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely develops the central moral-character bridge needed by the cumulative route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The premises and intended conclusion are clear, although the necessity of God as the unique foundation remains an implicit comparative claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The deductive form is clear, but the disputed grounding premise is treated more decisively than the supplied comparative support warrants.

charity.alternative: Objective morality might have a non-theistic realist foundation or exist as fundamental normative fact.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument must establish not merely that God can ground morality, but that objective values and duties require God.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is formally coherent, but its central necessity premise contains a material bridge from objective normativity to a divine foundation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The existence and divine-dependence premises receive mainly philosophical assertion in the selected support, with rival grounding accounts underexamined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly addresses the central bridge that must connect objective morality to God's goodness and is maximally relevant within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move defines objectivity and offers a divine ground, but it does not seriously compare the strongest non-theistic realist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig explicitly says the first argument does not determine moral character, then introduces the premise that objective moral values and duties would not exist without God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples' resulting belief are best explained by Jesus's resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly introduces his third numbered argument and develops it continuously until beginning the summary of his opening case.

response.rationale: Constructive opening move; it supplies the specifically Christian identification component through three historical claims and a resurrection inference, without an earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the central historical bridge from generic theism to Christian identification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three alleged facts and best-explanation conclusion are clear, though the relevant comparison class and evidential qualifications remain compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Best-explanation language permits comparison, but the excerpt states the historical claims and resurrection preference with limited uncertainty or rival analysis.

charity.alternative: The reports could reflect a combination of ordinary historical processes rather than a bodily resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: The resurrection must outperform natural combinations after accounting for testimony dependence and the prior rarity of miracles.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is coherent, but a material bridge remains from the three reported facts to resurrection as the superior explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific historical claims are supplied, yet documentation, independence, base-rate treatment, and serious comparison with alternatives remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central resurrection-identification bridge and is at the top of relevance within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies concrete facts but does not within this span fully address the strongest combined natural or testimony-based alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt enumerates the empty tomb, postmortem appearances to individuals and groups, and the disciples' resulting belief, then identifies resurrection as their best explanation.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: The immense scale and depth of apparently gratuitous animal and human suffering provide powerful evidence against an omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law, who announces one opening argument and develops the evidential problem of evil throughout this uninterrupted passage.

response.rationale: Constructive opening move; it advances the observational case that the magnitude of suffering is improbable under perfect goodness and has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the central evidential demand and directly supports the principal observational-suffering bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is expressly evidential and probabilistic, with suffering's scale and the need for adequate reasons clearly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that the evidence makes the hypothesis highly implausible rather than claiming a deductive contradiction, matching its observational warrant.

charity.alternative: A perfectly good God might possess morally sufficient reasons for every instance of suffering.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge is probabilistic: the total scale and depth must still be plausible under such reasons, not merely logically compatible with them.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from extensive apparently gratuitous suffering to reduced probability is coherent, with only the likelihood comparison left partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes representative animal and human suffering and a clear probabilistic warrant, though no systematic frequency model is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable central bridge that observed suffering provides evidential grounds against perfect goodness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly grants that adequate reasons could answer the challenge and focuses fairly on their aggregate plausibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law argues that every ounce of suffering would require an entirely adequate reason and that suffering across the eons has such depth and magnitude that this is highly implausible.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Good-God belief faces a symmetry challenge because observed suffering counts against it just as observed goodness counts against an otherwise parallel evil-God hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: Law remains the sole speaker and explicitly pivots from his evidential argument to an alternative evil-creator hypothesis and its mirrored problem.

components.text: The cosmological inference does not identify the transcendent creator's moral character.
The separate moral argument is the proposed source of an asymmetry favoring goodness.

response.rationale: The reply directly contacts the cosmological move's inability to discriminate good from evil, but it does not yet answer the moral argument that expressly purports to supply that discrimination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts the decisive scope limitation of the cosmological argument while leaving the moral-grounding component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is clear and carefully restricted to what the cosmological argument establishes about moral character.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The symmetry is posed as a comparative challenge and expressly limited to the morally neutral cosmological support.

charity.alternative: Craig's cumulative case does not rely on the cosmological argument alone to establish goodness.
charity.decisiveQualification: The symmetry objection defeats only that component unless the moral and resurrection arguments also fail to provide asymmetry.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity inference is coherent for morally neutral creator evidence and avoids inferring an evil creator from the cosmological argument.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant follows from the expressly limited conclusion of the cosmological case, but the broader observational comparison is not fully developed here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central no-moral-asymmetry bridge by exposing the cosmological component's neutrality, though it does not settle the moral argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: Law acknowledges the distinct arguments and carefully states that the cosmological component itself supplies no moral clue, though the broader case remains open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law explicitly says Craig's cosmological argument supports an evil-creator hypothesis as well as a good-creator hypothesis because it gives no clue about the creator's moral character.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Free will, stable natural laws, soul-making, inscrutable purposes, and afterlife compensation can be mirrored to explain goodness under an evil God, so those defenses do not distinguish the good-God hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: Law continuously develops mirrored versions of familiar theodicies within his opening turn, with no intervening change of speaker or topic ownership.

response.rationale: Constructive move; it develops mirrored free-will, natural-law, soul-making, unknown-purpose, and compensation defenses to test whether standard theodicies distinguish moral character.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies the central comparative mechanism underlying the evil-creator challenge in extensive and explicit form.

precisionFindings.rationale: The mirroring thesis and its intended scope are clear: these defenses fail as discriminators when materially parallel defenses remain available.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims failure of discrimination rather than strict identity of every hypothesis, a force appropriate to the constructed parallels.

charity.alternative: Individual good-God defenses may contain morally asymmetric premises that cannot genuinely be mirrored.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge succeeds only where the reversed defense preserves the relevant structure rather than merely exchanging moral labels.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative structure is consistent and supplies multiple material parallels, with only some defense-specific asymmetries left underexplored.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several representative theodicies are specifically mirrored and explained, though the move does not independently establish equal prior plausibility of the deity hypotheses.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and comprehensively supports the indispensable central bridge concerning mirrored defenses.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move works through several substantive parallels and presents recognizable versions of the defenses, though it does not prove every asymmetry irrelevant.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law explicitly reverses standard defenses involving free will and law-governed nature and indicates parallel treatments of soul-making, purposes, and compensation.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: If abundant goodness makes an evil God highly unlikely despite mirrored defenses, abundant suffering should likewise make a good God highly unlikely unless a relevant asymmetry is established.
moves.attributionBasis: Law concludes his opening case in a continuous passage explicitly framing the challenge he is placing before Craig for the ensuing response.

components.text: Craig must establish a relevant moral asymmetry rather than merely posit a good creator.
Morally neutral creator evidence cannot by itself block observational exclusion of either moral extreme.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the cumulative case's need for moral discrimination and presses the direct parity: if observed goodness excludes an evil creator despite defenses, suffering requires comparable treatment absent an asymmetry.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive asymmetry demand, but it poses rather than resolves the disputed grounding premise of the moral argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional parity claim, observational comparison, and exception for a relevant asymmetry are all explicitly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move concludes that the deity is unlikely on observational grounds and expressly conditions parity on the absence of a relevant asymmetry.

charity.alternative: Independent moral or historical evidence might make a good God substantially more probable than an evil creator.
charity.decisiveQualification: Observational parity controls only unless that independent evidence establishes a relevant and sufficiently strong asymmetry.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The parity challenge is explicit and internally consistent, with its conclusion correctly conditioned on failure to establish a relevant asymmetry.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparison uses the shared evidential method and mirrored defenses effectively, though the likelihood equivalence remains qualitative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level con bridge by stating why suffering and symmetry can defeat the cumulative case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move frames the strongest escape condition directly by asking for a relevant asymmetry rather than assuming none could exist.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law states that abundant goodness permits reasonable rejection of an evil God despite ingenious defenses, then asks why abundant suffering should not similarly count against a good God.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Observed suffering does not defeat God unless it is probable that God lacks morally sufficient reasons and that a better feasible world was available.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig's first response, and Craig directly identifies Law's evidential problem before presenting this uninterrupted initial rebuttal.

components.text: The evidential inference requires probability that God lacks morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering.
A better world must be genuinely feasible given providential purposes, not merely imaginable.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the probability warrant and supplies a possible providential purpose, but possibility alone does not establish that the observed suffering is probable or expected under perfect goodness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive probabilistic inference and feasible-world premise, but answers them only partially through an undeveloped possibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burden and feasible-world claims are clear, but the move shifts between what the atheist must prove and what is needed for an evidential probability inference.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply treats inability to disprove possible reasons as defeating a probabilistic argument, which overstates what the speculative purpose warrants.

charity.alternative: Suffering can be evidence against God without proving that sufficient reasons are impossible or highly improbable with certainty.
charity.decisiveQualification: An evidential challenge requires comparative likelihood, so merely possible reasons do not by themselves neutralize the evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The possible-purpose response is compatible with theism, but it does not validly move from possibility to defeat of the opposing probability inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposed world-maximizing salvific reason is speculative and is not supported by comparative evidence that this suffering was necessary or probable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central observational-suffering bridge by contesting the morally sufficient reason and feasible-world requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly calls the argument evidential but substantially raises its burden toward proof and does not preserve the alternative's probabilistic standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says Law must show that God probably lacks morally sufficient reasons and suggests that a world suffused with evil might maximize freely achieved salvation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Evil-God symmetry does not undermine theism because divine goodness is not inferred from an inventory of worldly goods, and an evil creator would not be worship-worthy God.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a continuous portion of Craig's explicitly introduced rebuttal, with first-person references to his own argument.

components.text: An evil creator is not worship-worthy and therefore is not literally God under Craig's definition.
Divine goodness is not inferred merely by counting worldly goods.
The observational parity still requires an evidential asymmetry rather than a terminological distinction.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the mirrored hypothesis and rejects an inductive route to divine goodness, but defining God as worship-worthy does not answer whether an evil creator is evidentially parallel.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts definitional and inductive components but leaves the decisive observational parity component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is recoverable, but shifting from evil God to evil creator introduces a material terminological issue without changing the hypothesis's evidential role.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The definitional exclusion is presented as decisive against a challenge whose central force concerns an evil creator's evidential symmetry.

charity.alternative: The evil-God label can denote an omnipotent evil creator without claiming that such a being deserves worship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Renaming the hypothesis does not remove the demand to explain why evidence treats the evil and good creators differently.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The worship-worthiness definition is internally consistent, but it is largely nonresponsive to the comparative inference and risks a terminological non sequitur.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim that goodness is noninductive is asserted without enough positive warrant here to establish the needed evidential asymmetry.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central mirrored-defenses bridge, although much of the attack is terminological rather than evidential.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move briefly allows an evil creator but relies materially on the worship-worthiness definition and omits the alternative's decisive evidential qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that a supreme object of religious attitudes must be morally excellent, concedes an evil creator can be conceived, and denies deriving divine goodness from worldly inventory.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: The evidential challenge can be framed solely in terms of apparently excessive suffering, so it neither presupposes objective evil nor depends upon moral realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's rebuttal, and Law explicitly identifies and answers Craig's claim that evil proves God.

components.text: The suffering argument need not assert objective evil or accept moral realism.
Apparently excessive suffering can ground a probabilistic challenge without an objective-evil premise.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the dependence claim as false and states the consequence: even a moral nihilist can formulate the evidential challenge using the quantity of suffering.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This diagnostic defeat explicitly identifies the disputed premise and preserves the evidential challenge without it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between suffering and objective evil is explicit, and the limited consequence for the evidential argument is clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual point is appropriately categorical: describing suffering and comparing its expected amount does not logically require moral realism.

charity.alternative: Calling suffering excessive may covertly invoke an objective normative standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument can instead compare observed suffering with what Craig's own good-God hypothesis predicts, without the atheist endorsing objective value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic distinction is explicit and valid: an internal likelihood critique need not commit its proponent to objective moral facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The support is principally conceptual and directly demonstrates how the argument can be restated solely in terms of observed suffering.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary bridge permitting a suffering argument without moral realism and is at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately addresses the strongest concern by grounding the internal evidential comparison in the theist's hypothesis rather than atheist moral commitment.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law explicitly says an atheist could be a moral nihilist and still run the evidential argument from the enormous amount of suffering compared with God's proposed purposes.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Craig has not established that objective moral values exist or that they require God, and combining those premises with the evidence of suffering may support moral skepticism rather than theism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Law's next rebuttal, and Law explicitly turns to Craig's arguments before sustaining a detailed critique of the moral argument.

components.text: Neither objective morality nor its alleged dependence on God has been adequately established.
The observed suffering may function as counterevidence within Craig's own moral premises.

response.rationale: The reply directly disputes both premises and proposes a countervailing inference from suffering, though its appeal to philosophical opinion does not itself resolve either premise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive premises and offers contrary reasoning, but the substantive alternative grounding case remains underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two premise challenges are clear, but the role of philosophical disagreement and suffering as counterevidence is somewhat compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The skeptical conclusion is broadly proportionate, although references to majority rejection and a mountain of evidence exceed the detailed support shown.

charity.alternative: Craig offers a metaphysical explanatory argument, not an appeal to philosophical consensus, for grounding objective morality in God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Disagreement can show the premise is unsettled but cannot by itself defeat the proposed grounding explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objections are compatible and relevant, but the move leaves a material bridge from disagreement and suffering to rejection of the premises.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The support relies substantially on named authority and reported consensus, while providing limited direct defense of an atheist-compatible moral ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable central divine-ground bridge by disputing both premises of the moral argument.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply restates the argument accurately but leans materially on authority and consensus while compressing Craig's strongest explanatory rationale.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law restates Craig's two-premise moral argument, cites broad philosophical rejection and Swinburne's contrary judgment, and links suffering to possible moral skepticism.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Baffling and apparently corroborated testimony is expected to arise occasionally even without miracles, so the resurrection reports provide little support unless they discriminate against that baseline expectation.
moves.attributionBasis: Law explicitly turns to the resurrection argument and carries the resulting analogy and evidential conclusion through the delivered lookahead.

components.text: Baffling testimony must discriminate against the baseline expectation that some such reports arise naturally.

response.rationale: The reply directly contacts the best-explanation inference by supplying a base-rate demand, but its paranormal analogy does not separately assess the three historical claims or their dependence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive discriminatory warrant while leaving several case-specific evidential components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The baseline-expectation objection and its limited claim about evidential support are clearly and explicitly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move cautiously argues for little support absent discrimination, rather than claiming that natural processes certainly explain the reports.

charity.alternative: The resurrection case may combine several independently supported facts in a uniquely significant historical context.
charity.decisiveQualification: The baseline objection must address whether that conjunction and context are substantially less expected under ordinary processes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The likelihood principle is sound and clearly applied, with a bounded gap in translating generic report frequency to this particular evidential conjunction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move gives an intelligible baseline analogy, but supplies little representative frequency evidence or detailed comparison with the specific resurrection reports.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central resurrection-identification bridge by challenging the reports' discriminatory force.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply targets the correct likelihood principle but underdevelops the strongest case-specific conjunction and contextual qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law states that hard-to-explain reports should occasionally arise without miracles, so one baffling case gives little support unless it is expected on resurrection and unexpected otherwise.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Atheism supplies no adequate account of objective moral values and duties, whereas God's nature and commands provide a transcendent foundation for them.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig continues his announced summation, addresses Law by name, and restates the premises and explanatory rationale of his moral argument.

components.text: Theism offers a transcendent explanation for objective moral status while Law supplies no alternative account.
The internal suffering argument does not itself answer the metaphysical grounding question.

response.rationale: The reply directly addresses the explanatory-grounding challenge and correctly distinguishes it from the suffering argument, but lack of an offered atheist account does not establish necessity of theism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive explanatory issue but only partially answers the rival-premise challenge because compatibility is treated as comparative superiority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory comparison and the proposed roles of divine nature and commands are recoverable and carefully limited to a better-foundation claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparative conclusion is qualified as better, but the absence of an articulated rival is insufficient by itself to establish superiority.

charity.alternative: Non-theistic moral realism may treat normative facts as fundamental even if Law did not develop that view here.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig may criticize Law's performance, but must still show why the divine account explains normativity better than a strong available rival.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The nature-and-command account is coherent as a candidate explanation, but its comparative superiority requires a material unstated exclusivity bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A specific theistic ground is offered, yet the warrant depends substantially on Law's omission rather than serious comparison with non-theistic realism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central no-moral-asymmetry bridge by supplying the intended theistic moral explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly notes the missing opposing explanation but omits the decisive qualification that a debate omission does not exhaust live metaphysical alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that a moral theory should explain the moral realm's objective status, says Law offered no account, and proposes God's nature and commands as a transcendent ground.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus's resurrection satisfies explanatory criteria better than natural alternatives and is rendered plausible by the religious-historical context of his life and claims.
moves.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Craig summation explicitly turns to the resurrection and contrasts his explanation with Law's paranormal-report analogy.

components.text: The resurrection claim must be compared by explanatory criteria and assessed in its distinctive religious-historical context.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the generic-base-rate objection with case-specific criteria and context, but it asserts that no natural explanation performs as well without demonstrating those comparisons in detail.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive discrimination demand and provides a relevant answer, though the comparative analysis remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory criteria, comparative conclusion, and contextual qualification are all clearly recoverable from the move.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as an explanatory judgment, but the strong comparative preference is supported mostly by assertion in this span.

charity.alternative: Generic baffling reports establish a relevant low base rate for false extraordinary testimony even in meaningful contexts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Context can raise plausibility only if it is itself more expected under resurrection than under ordinary religious development.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The case-specific rebuttal is coherent and identifies proper abductive criteria, with one material comparative bridge left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The criteria and context are relevant, but natural alternatives, independence, and prior probability are not substantively compared in the selected evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central cumulative-insufficiency bridge by defending the Christian identification component against the base-rate objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly accepts the caution generated by paranormal reports but does not fully address the alternative explanation of the allegedly significant context.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig accepts caution about paranormal claims, lists explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and ad hocness, then claims resurrection performs best and invokes Jesus's religious context.

moves.speaker: Stephen Law
moves.proposition: Even if a cosmological argument established a creator, it would supply no grounds for preferring an all-good creator over an all-evil creator and would not establish Craig's God.
moves.attributionBasis: A moderator question cues Law, who explicitly denies Craig's characterization of his position and explains the restricted scope of his debate strategy.

components.text: Even a successful cosmological argument would establish no preference between a good and evil creator.
Calling an evil creator nondivine does not add evidence for the creator's goodness.
A separate moral argument, not cosmology, must carry the moral-character inference.

response.rationale: The reply explicitly diagnoses Craig's alleged concession reading as mistaken and states the defeating consequence: the cosmological conclusion alone cannot establish Craig's morally specified God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This diagnostic defeat expressly identifies the scope error and preserves the legitimate distinction between creator existence and moral character.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes nonconcession, conditional creator existence, and the cosmological argument's morally neutral scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The restricted conclusion follows directly from the stated content of the cosmological argument and does not overclaim its overall falsity.

charity.alternative: Craig's cumulative case assigns moral character to the separate moral argument rather than the cosmological premise.
charity.decisiveQualification: Law's objection is expressly component-specific and does not purport to show that no later argument could establish goodness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope diagnosis is explicit, consistent, and directly resolves the alleged inference from conditional discussion to concession.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant rests on the expressly stated limited conclusion of Craig's own first argument and needs little additional factual support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central cumulative-components-insufficient bridge by isolating the cosmological component's inability to identify a good Christian God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately preserves the cumulative structure while insisting that the cosmological component itself is morally neutral.

moves.evidenceBasis: Law denies conceding a creator and explains that, even conditionally, Craig's first argument gives no grounds for preferring an all-good creator over an all-evil one.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The cosmological case is a deductive argument requiring denial of either the universe's beginning or its transcendent cause, rather than an appeal to gaps in scientific knowledge.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks whether Law's profession of ignorance is sufficient, and Craig answers in the first person while restating his deductive premises.

components.text: The cosmological case is deductive and cannot be answered merely by professing ignorance about origins.
Its deductive form still does not determine the cause's moral character.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses an ignorance-based objection as failing to deny either premise, but it does not contact Law's selected decisive claim that the resulting cause is morally neutral.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It defeats an adjacent epistemic response but leaves the selected move's principal moral-neutrality component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deductive alternatives and distinction from a scientific gap argument are clearly and stably stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that a valid deduction requires challenging a premise is appropriately categorical and explicitly distinguished from premise evidence.

charity.alternative: Law can grant the deductive form while disputing moral identification rather than answering with ignorance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defending deductive validity does not answer the separate claim that the conclusion is morally neutral.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The statement about deductive structure is explicit and valid, while carefully distinguishing premise support from a gaps inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move accurately restates its premises and philosophical form, though it does not add substantial defense of either disputed premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central transcendent-cause challenge, but only at the lower edge of the tier because it misses the target's moral-neutrality demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately treats an ignorance response but omits the decisive qualification in Law's strongest selected argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says an opponent must deny either the universe's beginning or the conditional transcendent-cause premise and distinguishes this philosophical deduction from filling scientific gaps.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Human cognitive limitations prevent reliable probability judgments that apparently gratuitous goods or evils lack sufficient purposes in an omniscient being's providential plan.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker refers back to a point previously made from Stephen Wykstra and develops Craig's characteristic skeptical-theist response concerning divine purposes.

components.text: Finite observers cannot reliably judge whether apparent goods or evils are gratuitous within omniscient providence.
The probability inference from apparently gratuitous suffering depends on cognitive access to divine purposes.
The same skeptical limit appears applicable to judgments about gratuitous good under an evil creator.

response.rationale: The reply directly attacks observational probability judgments by invoking cognitive limits, but it does not explain why that skepticism blocks the good-God inference without equally shielding an evil creator.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the key epistemic premise but leaves the decisive mirrored application and resulting symmetry unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cognitive-limits thesis is clear, but its unrestricted phrase 'any sort of probability judgment' makes its scope materially broader than defended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Limited access can weaken confidence, but the categorical bar on any probability judgment exceeds the support supplied and risks selective skepticism.

charity.alternative: Limited knowledge reduces confidence without eliminating ordinary comparative evidence, and the limit applies symmetrically to good and evil creators.
charity.decisiveQualification: To defeat parity, the epistemic restriction must be calibrated and must explain why it does not neutralize both observational exclusions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from limited cognition to some caution is coherent, but the move unsupportedly expands this into inability to make any probability judgment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Omniscient hidden purposes are possible, yet no evidence or calibrated principle establishes that ordinary likelihood judgments become wholly unreliable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the motion-level con bridge by challenging the observational inference central to both suffering and symmetry.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes human limitations but omits the strongest alternative's decisive symmetric and degree-sensitive qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig argues that an omniscient providential being may have inaccessible ends and concludes that humans cannot make probability judgments that apparent goods or evils are gratuitous.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The long-range consequences of historical events exceed human epistemic reach, so observers cannot know that God lacks sufficient reasons for permitting particular suffering.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer recalls Craig's earlier citation of James Clerk Maxwell and articulates a providential ripple-effect account of morally sufficient reasons for suffering.

components.text: Long-range consequences may conceal morally sufficient reasons for particular suffering.
Hidden historical consequences do not by themselves establish an asymmetry between good and evil creators.

response.rationale: The reply directly supplies a mechanism for epistemic limitation concerning particular suffering, but it establishes possibility rather than the comparative likelihood needed to neutralize aggregate evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the suffering inference through a concrete hidden-consequence mechanism while leaving the symmetry and probability demands unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ripple-effect mechanism, temporal limitation, and restricted inability to know particular reasons are explicitly and stably described.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move properly stresses uncertainty, but 'no way to know' is stronger than the plausible claim that distant consequences limit confidence.

charity.alternative: Unknown long-term consequences can coexist with strong aggregate evidence that extensive suffering is unlikely under perfect goodness.
charity.decisiveQualification: A possibility concerning particular cases does not automatically defeat a distribution-level or comparative likelihood argument.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical ripple mechanism coherently supports epistemic caution, but a material bridge remains from delayed consequences to broad evidential defeat.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanism is plausible but speculative, with no representative demonstration that such consequences supply adequate reasons for the suffering at issue.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary epistemic-limits bridge and ranks near the top of relevance within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a relevant mechanism but omits the strongest alternative's decisive distinction between case-level knowledge and aggregate evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig says historical events produce ripple effects whose morally sufficient providential purpose may not emerge within observers' lifetimes or locations.
